21.2.3 Properties

Proteins are complex organic compounds. The physical and chemical properties of proteins are,

1. Physical Properties of Proteins

Proteins are colourless and usually tasteless.

The proteins range in shape from simple crystalloid spherical structures to long fibrillar structures. Two shapes have been recognized: (a). Globular proteins: They are spherical in shape. (b). Fibrillar proteins: They are in thread-like structure.

The proteins generally have high molecular weights.

Protein denaturation is the changes in the properties of a protein or loss of biologic activity.

Like amino acids, the proteins are amphoteric in nature because they contain both acidic (–COOH) and basic (amino) group.

The solubility of proteins is influenced by pH.

All protein solutions rotate the plane of polarized light to the left, i.e., these are levorotatory.

2. Chemical Properties of Proteins

The chemical properties of proteins are,

Hydrolysis: Proteins are hydrolysed by a variety of hydrolytic agents, such as acidic agents and basic (alkaline) agents.

They react with both acids and bases.

They can be precipitated from their solutions by salts of heavy metals, heat and alcohols etc.

When proteins are strongly heated or treated with certain reagents they lose their structural organization and their biological functions. This is known as coagulation of proteins.

21.2.4 Importance of Proteins

Proteins are the most significant biological compounds of living beings. They play an important role in many fundamental biological processes and functions. They are very versatile and have many different functions in the body. These are most critical to life and perform different types of functions. Some of these are,

Proteins are the most abundant intra-cellular macromolecules and form more than 50% of the dry weight of most organisms.

Many of the proteins act as living catalysts called enzymes. Enzymes increase the rate of biological reactions to the extent required by the body.

They act as barrier such as skin and bacterial cell walls.

They act as storage depots, such as ferritin for iron storage in blood.

The nucleoproteins act as carrier of genetic information or characters. They serve as basis of inheritance of heredity characters from parents to off springs (in the form of genes).

Hormones are proteins in nature. They regulate the growth of living organism and control a number of other physiological functions.

Some proteins serve as carrier of different substances inside the body. For example, haemoglobin is a protein in red blood cells that acts as carrier of oxygen, ceruloplasmin, is a protein acts as carrier of copper in the blood plasma.

Figure 21.2 Different structure levels of proteins.

21.2.3 Properties

Proteins are complex organic compounds. The physical and chemical properties of proteins are,

1. Physical Properties of Proteins

Proteins are colourless and usually tasteless.

The proteins range in shape from simple crystalloid spherical structures to long fibrillar structures. Two shapes have been recognized: (a). Globular proteins: They are spherical in shape. (b). Fibrillar proteins: They are in thread-like structure.

The proteins generally have high molecular weights.

Protein denaturation is the changes in the properties of a protein or loss of biologic activity.

Like amino acids, the proteins are amphoteric in nature because they contain both acidic (–COOH) and basic (amino) group.

The solubility of proteins is influenced by pH.

All protein solutions rotate the plane of polarized light to the left, i.e., these are levorotatory.

2. Chemical Properties of Proteins

The chemical properties of proteins are,

Hydrolysis: Proteins are hydrolysed by a variety of hydrolytic agents, such as acidic agents and basic (alkaline) agents.

They react with both acids and bases.

They can be precipitated from their solutions by salts of heavy metals, heat and alcohols etc.

When proteins are strongly heated or treated with certain reagents they lose their structural organization and their biological functions. This is known as coagulation of proteins.

21.2.4 Importance of Proteins

Proteins are the most significant biological compounds of living beings. They play an important role in many fundamental biological processes and functions. They are very versatile and have many different functions in the body. These are most critical to life and perform different types of functions. Some of these are,

Proteins are the most abundant intra-cellular macromolecules and form more than 50% of the dry weight of most organisms.

Many of the proteins act as living catalysts called enzymes. Enzymes increase the rate of biological reactions to the extent required by the body.

They act as barrier such as skin and bacterial cell walls.

They act as storage depots, such as ferritin for iron storage in blood.

The nucleoproteins act as carrier of genetic information or characters. They serve as basis of inheritance of heredity characters from parents to off springs (in the form of genes).

Hormones are proteins in nature. They regulate the growth of living organism and control a number of other physiological functions.

Some proteins serve as carrier of different substances inside the body. For example, haemoglobin is a protein in red blood cells that acts as carrier of oxygen, ceruloplasmin, is a protein acts as carrier of copper in the blood plasma.
